transcript:
Meeting: Technical deep dive - Autoscaling & capacity planning
Date/Time: 2026-05-22 16:00 UTC
Duration: 62 minutes
Attendees: Alex Kim (Redwood AE), Priya Rao (Redwood SE), Marta Gonzales (Redwood), Jordan Lee (Atlas CTO), Maya Patel (Atlas ML Eng), Sam Torres (Atlas DevOps), Ibrahim Nadeem (Atlas SRE)

Summary (auto): Discussed autoscaling patterns and capacity planning for Atlas's latency-sensitive inference workloads. Covered reserved GPUs for baseline, burst handling strategies, queueing and batching trade-offs, KV cache warm pools, and VPC/on-prem constraints.

Topics: autoscaling, reserved capacity, burst policies, queueing models, batching, KV cache, quantization, VPC onboarding

[00:00] Alex: Hey everyone thanks for joining, quick intro - I'm Alex from Redwood, AE, with Priya our SE and Marta on solutions. Could each of you give a 1-min on what you're seeing on your side?
[00:18] Jordan: Yeah sure, Jordan here CTO at Atlas. We're rolling ML features into our triage pipeline card, it's latency-sensitive - p50 around 80ms target, p95 under 300ms, but currently we're spiky at peak and cost is blowing up.
[00:32] Maya: Maya - we run a fleet of inference containers on k8s, right now models are 7B and some 13B, using FP16 on prem GPUs, but cold starts and batching variability cause big p95 spikes.
[00:46] Sam: Sam, ops, we also have strict VPC controls - no egress allowed, KMS for keys, and need audit logs - so private deployment is likely.
[00:58] Priya: Great, thanks. Today we'll focus on autoscaling and capacity planning: baseline reserved GPUs, burst policies, queueing model decisions, batching windows and KV cache warm pools. We'll go into quantization tradeoffs and VPC operational constraints.

[01:20] Alex: Quick note - when we say reserved capacity here we mean a baseline pool of dedicated GPUs that you commit to, for predictability and warm caches; burst can be handled several ways: short-term shared hosted pool, pre-warmed spot nodes, or queueing with SLO-based admission.
[01:40] Jordan: What's the recommendation for a baseline vs burst ratio? We want cost control but can't sacrifice the p95 target.

[01:50] Priya: In our experience for latency SLOs p50 targets -> keep most requests served off baseline. For p95 you need headroom: typical pattern is 70-80% baseline utilization with 20-30% reserved for headroom; bursts go to either a warm burst pool or spill to hosted where latency degrades slightly. If you can't use hosted spill due to VPC, then we recommend a small warm pool of pre-warmed GPUs or configuration of faster autoscale thresholds.

[02:20] Maya: Would pre-warmed GPUs significantly increase cost? We're trying to justify financials to leadership.
[02:26] Priya: Yes there's a trade-off. Pre-warmed GPUs have cost like reserved capacity but only active when used; you can configure warm pool size and cooldowns. Another hybrid is reserved baseline + short-lived spot nodes for extreme spikes; but spot reliability depends on your tolerance. Quantization and batching can reduce token cost, so we also run those optimizations in parallel.

[02:50] Sam: On the k8s side, we currently use HPA on CPU/memory and a custom scaler that watches GPU-util. Cold starts are long because we rehydrate KV cache. Any suggestions?
[03:04] Priya: Two things: 1) hold a warm KV cache pool — keep a set of pods with model weights loaded and KV cache primed for common prefixes; 2) reduce model load time via image layering and local NVMe cache. For k8s autoscaling, custom metrics (like queue length or in-flight tokens) are better signals than GPU utilization alone.

[03:30] Alex: Let's talk queueing models for admission control. For a single class of traffic, an M/M/c model is a starting point - arrival rate lambda, service rate mu, c servers. For multi-class (interactive + background) we use priority queues and admission policies. The point is to model p95 under bursts and set SLO-based admission thresholds.

[03:58] Jordan: Can you quantify mu for our models? How many requests/sec per GPU for 7B vs 13B?
[04:06] Priya: Ballpark numbers: for 7B on an A10-like GPU you might see 8-12 concurrent tokens streams with batching; throughput ~40-80 rps depending on seq length and batching window. 13B is roughly 40-60% of that. These numbers vary with quantization: int8 can push throughput up ~1.5-2x if accuracy is acceptable.

[04:36] Maya: Batching window - we worry about latency. What's a safe batching window?
[04:42] Priya: Typical is 20-50ms batching window for interactive apps. Short windows give less aggregation but keep p50 low; longer windows raise p50 but lower cost. Also continuous batching + adaptive batching is useful - if arrival rate high, you go to larger batches automatically.

[05:00] Marta: We also should mention prefix/KV cache. If you can route requests for similar prefixes to the same warmed instance, you can avoid recomputation. That reduces p95 a lot. But it requires sticky routing or a routing policy keyed on conversation id.

[05:18] Sam: We have sticky sessions for stateful services; on-prem folks worry about scaling sticky routing though.
[05:23] Priya: Sticky plus a bounded reroute window is fine. Also consider global cache sharding for large customer footprints.

[05:40] Jordan: For reserved GPUs what's the recommended sizing exercise? We don't have clear traffic curves yet.
[05:46] Alex: We typically ask for a traffic profile: baseline RPS, peak RPS, percentiles (5,50,95), sequence length distribution, and acceptable SLOs. From that we run a capacity planner that outputs GPU count for baseline and warm pool sizing. We'll share a spreadsheet that models cost vs latency with variables for batching, quantization, and warm pool size.

[06:12] Priya: I'll call out a simple heuristic: start with enough GPUs to hit baseline at 60-70% utilization at your p50. That leaves headroom. Then simulate burst scenarios; if VPC prevents external spillover, add warm pool capacity that can absorb 95th percentile spikes within cooldown window.

[06:32] Maya: Can Redwood support localized private control plane so we keep keys on-prem?
[06:38] Alex: Yes, Redwood Private supports a customer-managed control plane with KMS integrations and audit logs. For air-gapped we ship an on-prem package. There are extra ops steps for upgrades but it's supported.

[06:52] Ibrahim: One constraint: our security team requires no outbound connections from inference nodes. That rules out spilling to hosted. How does Redwood handle this?
[06:59] Priya: In that case we recommend sizing baseline + warm pool and tighter autoscale thresholds. To reduce cost, layering quantization and aggressive batching can offset the additional reserved capacity. Also you can set internal fallback model variants — smaller quantized models for degraded mode.

[07:20] Jordan: Fallbacks sound useful. How seamless is model variant fallback?
[07:24] Priya: Redwood runtime supports model variant routing; you can set drop-in fallback policies that route to a lower-capacity quantized variant if latency/queue thresholds exceed. That degrades quality but keeps latency.

[07:40] Marta: Let's drill into queueing & admission control: we recommend using token-based concurrency as a metric. Treat each token generation as a service unit; your admission controller enforces a max in-flight tokens per GPU, which maps to an effective mu in your M/M/c model.

[07:58] Maya: Example numbers?
[08:02] Priya: Say a GPU can handle 8 in-flight token streams with average of 50 tokens per request at 50ms per token — you'd compute mu accordingly. But simpler: use measured RPS under real traffic for each GPU and extrapolate. We provide tooling to run synthetic load with varying seq lengths to build that curve.

[08:28] Jordan: What about autoscaler config: thresholds and cool-downs? We saw flappy nodes before.
[08:34] Priya: Use two-stage scaling: fast scale-up (low threshold, e.g., queue length > X) with small steps, and slower scale-down with longer cooldowns to avoid churn. Warm pools help reduce the impact of scale-up latency. Use rate-limited scaling to control cost.

[08:52] Sam: Network and storage: what's the best practice for model artifacts and KV cache on-prem?
[08:58] Marta: Keep model weights on local NVMe for fastest load; use a separate persistent cache for KV that's mounted; prefer ephemeral warm pods that keep KV in memory not on disk. For model updates, use blue/green deploys to avoid cache misses during rollout.

[09:16] Jordan: Quantization: how much accuracy drop should we expect for int8 on our models?
[09:21] Priya: Depends on model and eval set. For many open models, post-training quantization to int8 with per-channel calibration yields small quality degradation (a few percentage points on some metrics). We recommend running evals tied to your prompt set before committing. Redwood Optimize can suggest quant profiles per workload.

[09:38] Maya: If we quantize, does that change capacity planning?
[09:41] Priya: Yes, quantization increases throughput so fewer GPUs needed for baseline; it also reduces warm pool size and reduces scale-up latency since smaller memory footprint helps faster instance startup. But you must validate quality.

[09:56] Jordan: Can we do progressive rollout of quantized models?
[10:00] Alex: Absolutely — canary first, then A/B and automatic rollback on quality regressions using eval hooks. That's part of Redwood Console features.

[10:14] Maya: For burst policies, you mentioned spill to hosted vs queueing. Can you outline pros/cons?
[10:20] Priya: Spill to hosted: pros - lower cost, elastic; cons - network egress if private, slightly higher latency variance. Queueing/admission: pros - predictable latency for admitted requests, prevents unexpected egress; cons - some requests get throttled and need graceful degradation. Warm pool: pros - low latency, local; cons - cost of reserved warm capacity.

[10:48] Jordan: If we choose warm pool approach how do we size it?
[10:52] Priya: Use historical peak over baseline and run simulations. As a rule of thumb, size warm pool for 95th percentile additional load over 60-minute window if you expect sustained bursts; for short spikes (seconds) smaller warm pools plus fast spin-up is okay. We'll send the spreadsheet with model parameters.

[11:12] Sam: For k8s autoscaler we need recommendations for resource requests/limits for model pods.
[11:18] Priya: Make GPU the primary resource request, set CPU for pre/post processing and a small baseline memory for KV. Avoid overcommit on GPU. Use separate sidecars for heavy preprocessing so the model container remains stable.

[11:34] Jordan: Any tips on throttling and client-side retry/backoff?
[11:38] Marta: Implement 429 with Retry-After, and an exponential backoff with jitter. Better: client-side queueing and smoothing to avoid thundering herd on peaks. Also expose adaptive rate/credits so clients can back off gracefully.

[11:58] Maya: For observability, what signals do you recommend tracking?
[12:02] Priya: p50/p95 latency, token-level throughput, batch size distribution, queue length, in-flight tokens, GPU util, cache hit rate, cold start count, and model variant routing ratios. Alert on sustained queue growth and cache miss spikes.

[12:24] Alex: Let's do a quick worked example with numbers from Atlas. Maya provided a sample: baseline 200 rps, peak 800 rps, seq length average 60 tokens, p95 latency target 300ms.
[12:40] Priya: With those numbers, if a 7B model on your on-prem GPU gives ~60 rps per GPU at target batching, baseline 200 rps implies ~4 GPUs (200/60 ~ 3.3 -> round up). For peak 800 rps, you'd need ~14 GPUs without batching/quantization; with int8 or larger batch sizes you can reduce to ~8-10. Warm pool for peaks could be ~6 GPUs sized to absorb 95th percentile. We'll model exacts in the spreadsheet.

[13:12] Jordan: How do we handle mixed model fleet (7B + 13B)?
[13:16] Priya: Dedicated pools per model family are simplest. If you co-locate, use admission control per pool and prefer routing to lighter models for degraded requests. Also consider autoscaling policies per pool with cross-pool fallback rules.

[13:34] Sam: Any considerations for HSM/KMS integration during autoscaling? Keys must be available to new nodes.

[13:40] Alex: For private/on-prem, you can either pre-provision keys on warm pool nodes or have a secure mounting mechanism for KMS tokens. We support integrations and provide runbooks for key rotation that don't require exposing master keys to ephemeral nodes.

[14:00] Maya: We also need compliance logs for audits - does Redwood produce audit trails for scaling events?
[14:06] Marta: Yes, Redwood Private emits audit logs for deployment and scaling events, can integrate with SIEM and long-term retention as an add-on.

[14:18] Jordan: Can we run a pilot with mixed traffic and measure p95 improvements with KV warm pools and quantization?
[14:22] Alex: Yes that's the recommended next step. We'll get the spreadsheet first, then plan a two-week pilot where you provide sample traffic and we'll run the benchmark in your environment (private or hybrid).

[14:34] Maya: About metrics and dashboards, can Redwood Console show token-level cost breakdown?
[14:38] Priya: Yep, per-token cost, per-route and per-model breakdowns, and traces showing cache hit/miss per request.

[14:48] Jordan: Any gotchas with GPU types? We have a mix of older cards and some newer ones.

[14:53] Priya: Performance varies a lot. Newer Ampere/Blackwell style GPUs give better throughput and kernel support; older cards may limit batch sizes. Our runtime selects kernels based on hardware and model and will suggest quantization and batch windows per GPU class. Avoid mixing very different GPU types in the same pool unless you tag and autoscale per-class.

[15:18] Sam: In terms of orchestration, can Redwood integrate with our cluster autoscaler?
[15:22] Alex: Yes, we integrate with k8s Cluster Autoscaler and support custom scalers. The runtime can emit custom metrics for autoscaler to act on. We usually recommend a control-plane orchestrator that handles model placement and warm pools while leaving infra autoscale to CA.

[15:40] Priya: Quick note on billing: for Dedicated/Reserved we offer committed monthly plans. Warm pools are billed as reserved until turned off. For spot transient nodes we bill usage only. We'll include pricing scenarios in the spreadsheet.

[15:58] Jordan: Great. I think the main risk is our no-egress policy. We'll need a thorough sizing exercise to justify the reserved capacity.

[16:06] Alex: Understood. We'll prioritize a spreadsheet that models worst-case and typical-case with quantization and batching toggles. Also we'll include a recommended warm pool size and scaling recipe for k8s.

[16:20] Maya: Can you also include an experiment plan for A/Bing quantized variant vs FP16 to measure quality impacts?

[16:25] Priya: Yes, we'll propose an eval harness and automated rollback criteria. Redwood Optimize can run regression alerts against your prompt set.

[16:36] Jordan: Last Q - how do we safely do DB/CV connections when pods scale? Any network best practices?

[16:41] Marta: Use internal VPC endpoints, maintain connection pools with proxies, and avoid creating new DB connections on each pod start. For ephemeral pods use connection poolers or a shared gateway.

[16:56] Alex: Ok let's recap real quick - action items and next steps. We'll send the capacity planning spreadsheet, benchmark scripts, and scheduling link for the pilot. Atlas to provide traffic profiles and SLOs.

[17:10] Jordan: Sounds good. Thanks everyone.

[17:14] Alex: Thanks - we'll follow up by Monday with the spreadsheet and a proposed pilot window.

[17:20] (call ends)

Notes: There are typical transcription imperfections (names sometimes garbled) and some speaker attribution may be approximate. References: capacity-planner.xlsx (sent), SOC2 and VPC onboarding doc (link to be shared), benchmark scripts repo (link).
